subtopic_detail: Persistent organism after a first line eradication regimen confirmed by breath testing
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 54 year old man who had a duodenal ulcer found at endoscopy four months ago with biopsy confirmed Helicobacter pylori. He completed a seven day course of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin, taking every dose.

He returns because his epigastric pain has recurred. A urea breath test performed eight weeks after treatment, with his proton pump inhibitor withheld for two weeks beforehand, is positive. He has no penicillin allergy, has never taken a macrolide before that course, and has no alarm features with no weight loss, no vomiting, no dysphagia and no melaena. He does not smoke and takes no non steroidal anti inflammatory medication.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no mass, no lymphadenopathy, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Urea breath test positive eight weeks after treatment with proton pump inhibitor withheld two weeks, haemoglobin 146 g/L (130-170), previous endoscopy showing a duodenal ulcer with biopsy confirmed Helicobacter pylori

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: A second line regimen that avoids clarithromycin, using different antibiotics for a longer treatment course
options.rationale: Failure of a clarithromycin containing regimen taken with full adherence indicates macrolide resistance, and that agent must not be reused because resistance is stable and reduces eradication rates sharply. Australian practice moves to a bismuth based quadruple regimen or to a levofloxacin containing regimen, given for fourteen days rather than seven. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Repeat the identical seven day regimen for a further fourteen days to overcome incomplete organism clearance
options.rationale: Extending a regimen containing an antibiotic to which the organism is resistant does not overcome that resistance, and clarithromycin resistance is the commonest reason for first line failure. Reuse also drives further resistance without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Long term proton pump inhibitor treatment alone with a plan to reassess his symptoms after six months
options.rationale: Acid suppression heals ulcers but leaves the organism in place, so ulcers recur and the long term gastric cancer risk associated with persistent infection is unchanged. Eradication remains the objective in a patient with a proven ulcer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Repeat gastroscopy with gastric biopsies for culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing before treating
options.rationale: Culture directed therapy is genuinely useful and is recommended after two or more failed courses or where local resistance is high. Committing to a repeat endoscopy after a single failure, when an effective empirical second line regimen exists, is more invasive than the situation requires. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Repeat the urea breath test in a further three months since the earlier result may reflect residual organism
options.rationale: The test was performed correctly at eight weeks with the acid suppressant withheld for two weeks, which is exactly the protocol designed to avoid a false result. Repeating it delays treatment of a confirmed persistent infection in a man with a symptomatic ulcer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Eradication of Helicobacter pylori matters because it heals ulcers, prevents recurrence and reduces the long term risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma. Australian first line therapy is a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin, and success has fallen as macrolide resistance has risen. Confirmation of eradication requires a urea breath test or faecal antigen test at least four weeks after finishing antibiotics and with the acid suppressant withheld for two weeks, since both antibiotics and acid suppression produce false negative results. When a clarithromycin containing regimen fails in an adherent patient, resistance is assumed and that agent is not reused, with second line options being bismuth based quadruple therapy or a levofloxacin containing regimen, and a fourteen day duration preferred. Culture with susceptibility testing is reserved for repeated failure.
key_points: Confirm eradication at least four weeks after antibiotics with acid suppression withheld two weeks
Failure of an adherent clarithromycin regimen implies macrolide resistance
Never reuse clarithromycin after a failed course containing it
Second line options are bismuth quadruple therapy or a levofloxacin regimen for fourteen days
Culture directed therapy is reserved for two or more failures
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about any macrolide taken for a chest or sinus infection in previous years before choosing first line therapy, because a single prior exposure substantially raises the probability of clarithromycin resistance and is the most useful piece of history for predicting whether the standard regimen will work.

subtopic_detail: Recurrent hair pulling with visible loss and mounting tension before pulling
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 19 year old woman referred by her general practitioner with patchy hair loss on the scalp. She admits she pulls hair out, mostly while studying at night, and has done so for four years.

She describes a building sense of tension before pulling and relief immediately afterwards, and says she often does not register having started. She has begun wearing a beanie indoors and has stopped going to the gym because of the visible bald patches. She has no fixed belief that anything is living in her scalp, no intrusive contamination or checking thoughts, and no rituals. She has never eaten the hair. Her mood is generally reactive and she denies persistent low mood, sleeps adequately and continues at university. Examination shows irregular patches of broken hairs of differing lengths with no scaling, no scarring and no inflammation.

data_table.Examination: Irregular scalp patches with hairs broken at varying lengths, no scale, no erythema, no scarring alopecia, eyebrows and eyelashes intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Supportive counselling with advice to keep her hands occupied and to reduce her overall study related stress
options.rationale: General stress advice is well intentioned but lacks the specific components that make behavioural treatment work, namely detailed self monitoring and a trained competing response. Non specific support has not been shown to reduce pulling in trials. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Habit reversal training delivered as a structured behavioural programme with awareness and competing response work
options.rationale: Hair pulling preceded by tension and followed by relief, with insight preserved and no obsessional content, is a body focused repetitive behaviour for which habit reversal training is the treatment with the strongest evidence. The programme teaches awareness of the antecedent urge and substitution of an incompatible motor response, and it outperforms medication in comparative studies. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor titrated to the higher dose range used in obsessive compulsive disorder
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder but have performed poorly in trials of hair pulling, where results have been inconsistent and often no better than placebo. They are considered when a comorbid mood or anxiety disorder is present. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: A low dose antipsychotic prescribed to reduce the compulsive quality of the behaviour she describes
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation has limited evidence in this condition and carries metabolic and movement adverse effects that are hard to justify in a healthy young woman. It also implies a psychotic mechanism, and her insight is fully preserved. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Referral to dermatology for scalp biopsy and topical treatment of the areas of visible hair loss
options.rationale: Biopsy is used when the cause of alopecia is uncertain or when a scarring process is suspected, and the appearance of broken hairs at differing lengths without scale or scarring is already characteristic. Topical treatment does not address the behaviour producing the loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania is classified with obsessive compulsive and related disorders and involves recurrent hair pulling causing visible loss, with repeated attempts to stop and significant distress or impairment. It differs from obsessive compulsive disorder because the behaviour is not driven by an obsession and is not performed to neutralise a feared outcome, and it differs from delusional parasitosis because insight is intact. Pulling is frequently automatic, occurring during sedentary focused activities, and this is why self monitoring is a central treatment component. Habit reversal training, often delivered within a broader behavioural framework, is the first line intervention and has the best evidence, with medication reserved largely for comorbidity. Ingestion of pulled hair must be asked about directly because a trichobezoar can cause gastric outlet obstruction and requires surgical management.
key_points: Tension before pulling with relief afterwards and preserved insight defines the disorder
Absence of obsessions separates it from obsessive compulsive disorder
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms medication
Serotonergic antidepressants are for comorbid mood or anxiety disorder
Ask about hair ingestion because a trichobezoar is a surgical problem
explanation.pearls: Ask directly whether she swallows the hair after pulling, because trichophagia occurs in a minority and can produce a gastric trichobezoar with a tail extending into the small bowel, presenting with early satiety, vomiting and weight loss that is easily attributed to an eating disorder instead.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Intense yearning and preoccupation with a deceased spouse more than a year after the death
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 61 year old woman fifteen months after her husband died of pancreatic cancer. Her daughter has brought her because she has left his clothes hanging in the wardrobe, talks to his photograph for hours daily and has not returned to the choir she led for twenty years.

She describes an unrelenting ache to be with him and says she cannot accept that he is gone, replaying the days before his death repeatedly. She feels her own life has no purpose without him but says clearly that she does not want to die and would never harm herself. She has not lost weight, describes her appetite as reasonable, and enjoys her grandchildren's visits while feeling guilty afterwards for having enjoyed them. She sleeps six hours most nights and has no diurnal variation of mood, no psychomotor slowing and no pervasive anhedonia.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking of her husband, reactive affect with grandchildren mentioned, normal psychomotor activity, no perceptual disturbance, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine to help her tolerate the distress of sorting his belongings
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines given during bereavement have been associated with poorer grief outcomes and carry dependence and falls risk in this age group. Avoidance of distressing reminders is part of what maintains the disorder, and sedation reinforces it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange neuropsychological assessment given her withdrawal from a long standing leadership role in the choir
options.rationale: Cognitive assessment is warranted where there is memory impairment, disorientation or executive decline, and her cognition is intact with a clear account of her own state. Withdrawal here reflects grief related avoidance rather than cognitive change. (Source: RANZCP: Grief and bereavement)

options.text: Refer for a structured grief focused psychological therapy and arrange regular review of her progress
options.rationale: Persistent intense yearning and preoccupation with the deceased beyond twelve months, with functional impairment out of keeping with her cultural norms, meets criteria for prolonged grief disorder, and targeted grief focused psychotherapy has better outcomes than generic supportive therapy or antidepressant treatment alone. Her reactive affect, preserved appetite and absent anhedonia distinguish this from a major depressive episode. (Source: RANZCP: Grief and bereavement)

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review the response to treatment after six weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants treat a comorbid depressive episode when one is present but have not been shown to resolve the core yearning and preoccupation of prolonged grief. Her mood remains reactive with preserved appetite and no anhedonia, which argues against a depressive episode. (Source: RANZCP: Grief and bereavement)

options.text: Reassure her daughter that this is normal bereavement and that no specific intervention is required now
options.rationale: Ordinary grief loosens over the first year and does not typically leave someone unable to return to valued roles fifteen months on. Framing marked persistent impairment as normal denies her access to a treatment with demonstrated benefit. (Source: RANZCP: Grief and bereavement)

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder is diagnosed when intense yearning for the deceased or preoccupation with them persists beyond twelve months in adults, accompanied by symptoms such as disbelief, identity disruption, emotional numbness, avoidance of reminders and an inability to re engage with life, and causes clinically significant impairment beyond what cultural and religious norms would expect. It is distinguished from a major depressive episode by the focus on the deceased rather than pervasive worthlessness, by affect that remains reactive to positive stimuli, and by the frequent preservation of appetite and interest in specific relationships. It is distinguished from ordinary grief by duration, intensity and functional impairment rather than by the presence of sadness. Grief focused psychological therapies have the strongest evidence, and medication is added for comorbid depression or post traumatic stress rather than as primary treatment. Benzodiazepines should be avoided because they reinforce avoidance and have been associated with worse outcomes.
key_points: The twelve month threshold applies in adults, with six months used in children
Yearning focused on the deceased differs from the pervasive worthlessness of depression
Reactive affect and preserved appetite argue against a major depressive episode
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms generic support and medication alone
Benzodiazepines reinforce avoidance and are associated with poorer outcomes
explanation.pearls: Screen for suicidal ideation at every review even when the presentation looks like grief rather than depression, because a wish to be reunited with the deceased is a recognised and specific risk pathway in prolonged grief disorder and is often disclosed only when asked about in those exact terms.

subtopic_detail: Long standing difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep with daytime consequences
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 44 year old accountant who has struggled to sleep for two years, taking around ninety minutes to fall asleep and lying awake for an hour or more in the early hours. He asks directly for sleeping tablets, saying a friend takes them.

He goes to bed at 9 pm to give himself the best chance and stays there until 7 am, spending much of that time checking the clock and calculating how much sleep he will get. He drinks one coffee in the morning, no alcohol, and stops screen use an hour before bed. He denies snoring and his partner reports no witnessed pauses or leg movements. His mood is not persistently low, he has no anhedonia, and he denies worry outside the bedroom. His body mass index is 24 kg per square metre and thyroid function and iron studies are normal.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg per square metre, Mallampati class 2, no goitre, normal mental state examination with euthymic reactive affect
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.5 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), ferritin 110 micrograms/L (30-300), haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-170)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Low dose amitriptyline taken nightly for its sedating effect with review of tolerance after one month
options.rationale: Sedating antidepressants are widely used off label but carry anticholinergic effects, daytime sedation, weight gain and cardiac conduction risk, with modest evidence in primary insomnia. They are considered when depression coexists, which is not the case here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prolonged release melatonin taken two hours before bed with advice to maintain his current bedtime routine
options.rationale: Prolonged release melatonin has a modest effect and is registered in Australia mainly for insomnia in adults over fifty five. It also does not address the excessive time in bed and conditioned arousal that are maintaining his problem. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Referral for overnight polysomnography to exclude an underlying primary sleep disorder before treatment
options.rationale: Sleep studies are indicated where the history suggests sleep disordered breathing, periodic limb movements or a parasomnia, and none of those features are present with a favourable airway and no partner reported events. Routine testing in uncomplicated insomnia does not change management. (Source: RACGP: Insomnia)

options.text: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including sleep restriction and stimulus control components
options.rationale: Chronic insomnia without another sleep, medical or psychiatric disorder is treated first with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, which is more effective than hypnotic medication in the long term and does not carry tolerance or dependence. His ten hours in bed for far less sleep, with clock watching and sleep effort, is precisely the pattern that sleep restriction and stimulus control are designed to reverse. (Source: RACGP: Insomnia)

options.text: A short acting benzodiazepine receptor agonist prescribed nightly for four weeks with a planned taper
options.rationale: Hypnotics work in the short term and have a place for acute situational insomnia, but nightly use in chronic insomnia leads to tolerance, rebound on withdrawal and dependence, with falls and cognitive effects. They are not the first line for a two year problem. (Source: RACGP: Insomnia)

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia disorder requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep at least three nights a week for three months or more, with daytime consequences and adequate opportunity to sleep. Assessment excludes sleep disordered breathing, restless legs, circadian disorders, substances and psychiatric comorbidity, and iron and thyroid studies are reasonable screens. The condition is maintained by increased time in bed, conditioned arousal linking the bed with wakefulness, and effortful sleep behaviours such as clock watching, all of which are targeted directly by cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia. That therapy is first line in Australian and international guidance because it produces durable improvement without tolerance or dependence, and it is available through trained therapists and validated digital programmes. Hypnotic medication is reserved for short term use in acute situational insomnia or as a temporary adjunct, with clear discussion of duration at the outset.
key_points: Three months of difficulty with daytime consequences defines chronic insomnia disorder
Excess time in bed and conditioned arousal maintain the problem
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and durable
Hypnotics are for short term situational use, not for chronic insomnia
Sleep studies are for suspected breathing, movement or parasomnia disorders
explanation.pearls: Warn patients that sleep restriction transiently worsens daytime sleepiness in the first one to two weeks as time in bed is cut back towards actual sleep time, because dropping out during that window is the commonest reason the therapy fails and forewarning substantially improves completion.

subtopic_detail: Multiple motor and vocal tics with a premonitory urge in an adolescent
stem:
You are the child and adolescent psychiatry registrar seeing a 14 year old boy whose mother is distressed by his blinking, head jerking and repeated throat clearing. These began at seven, wax and wane, and have never been absent for more than a few weeks at a time.

He describes an uncomfortable building feeling in his neck and throat that is relieved once the movement happens, and he can hold the tics back for a few minutes in class before they come out in a burst afterwards. He is doing well academically, has friends, and is not bothered by the tics himself, though he is embarrassed when they occur during oral presentations. He has no obsessions, no compulsions and no attentional difficulties reported by teachers. His neurological examination is normal and he takes no medication or stimulant.

data_table.Examination: Frequent eye blinking, head jerking and throat clearing observed during interview, suppressible briefly on request, normal tone power reflexes and coordination, no chorea, no dystonia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start a low dose antipsychotic such as risperidone and titrate according to the frequency of the tics
options.rationale: Dopamine blocking agents suppress tics effectively but carry weight gain, metabolic effects, sedation and movement adverse effects, so they are reserved for tics causing significant pain, injury or functional impairment. This boy is functioning well academically and socially. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Advise him to suppress the tics whenever possible in public so that the habit gradually extinguishes itself
options.rationale: Effortful suppression is exhausting, does not extinguish tics and typically produces a rebound burst afterwards, which he already describes. Behavioural treatment works by substituting a competing response rather than by simple suppression. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with copper studies to investigate a secondary cause of tics
options.rationale: Investigation for a secondary cause is triggered by abnormal neurological findings, sudden onset in an older patient, or an atypical movement disorder such as chorea or dystonia. A typical waxing and waning course from childhood with a normal examination does not require it. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Start clonidine at low dose in the evening and increase gradually while monitoring his blood pressure
options.rationale: Clonidine is a reasonable pharmacological option with a more favourable adverse effect profile than antipsychotics, particularly when attention deficit hyperactivity disorder coexists. It remains medication for a boy whose tics are not causing significant impairment, so behavioural treatment comes first. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Psychoeducation for the family and school with referral for a behavioural therapy programme for tics
options.rationale: Multiple motor tics with at least one vocal tic persisting more than a year from childhood onset, with a premonitory urge and brief suppressibility, is Tourette syndrome, and where function is largely preserved the first step is education plus a behavioural programme. Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics teaches awareness of the premonitory urge and a competing response, and it works without the metabolic and movement risks of medication. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

explanation.summary: Tourette syndrome requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, present for more than a year with onset before eighteen, and typically follows a waxing and waning course that peaks in early adolescence and improves in many by adulthood. A premonitory urge relieved by the tic, and brief voluntary suppressibility followed by rebound, are characteristic and help distinguish tics from chorea, dystonia and stereotypies. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder both common and often causing more impairment than the tics themselves, so they must be screened for at every assessment. First line management for tics that are not causing significant impairment is psychoeducation for family and school plus behavioural therapy, specifically comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics. Medication is added when tics cause pain, injury, or substantial functional or social impairment.
key_points: Premonitory urge with brief suppressibility and rebound characterises tics
Waxing and waning course peaking in early adolescence is typical
Screen for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder
Behavioural therapy with psychoeducation is first line when impairment is limited
Medication is reserved for pain, injury or substantial impairment
explanation.pearls: Ask what causes the most impairment rather than what is most visible, because comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder more often drive academic and social difficulty than the tics do, and treating those conditions can transform function even when the tics are unchanged.
